_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Working Lands & Industry' — forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture, the resource economy that defines the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; wildlife content with no agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Trade-press journalism counts fully: equipment, markets, and operations coverage is a real fit, not a near-zero. A BC tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent working-lands journalism. BC/Cariboo forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture stories land here (mill closures, beetle kill, BCTS, Cariboo ranchers and water rights, local mine operations, Cariboo Cattlemen) — and so does outstanding national trade reporting with real operational or economic depth.
- 55-79: Solid resource-economy journalism anywhere in Canada or beyond — Western Producer or Northern Miner-style coverage of farm machinery, harvest technology, livestock and commodity markets, mining operations and exploration, AgTech and precision agriculture, silviculture, sawmills, drone survey work, mine automation, and labour/workforce stories in these industries. Most genuine trade journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Broader agriculture, forestry, or mining news with clear working-lands relevance but thin reporting — general farm economics, international resource-industry briefs, climate impacts on working lands.
- 15-29: Tangential mentions — a business, policy, or science story that touches forestry/agriculture/mining in passing, or Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.

ANCHORS: 'Williams Lake sawmill cuts second shift as beetle-kill supply dwindles' → 95. 'New John Deere baler cuts hay-drying time by a third' → 70. 'Cattle futures slip on weaker export demand' → 60. 'Global copper prices hit two-year high' → 40.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Conservative Party released a fully costed platform on Sunday afternoon, projecting that under a Tory government, the deficit will fall from $13.7 billion this year to $10.8 billion by 2029, aided by the party’s forecast of spectacular 3.2 per cent economic growth. This assumes 2.5 per cent growth this year, 2.8 per cent next year, and 3.2 per cent in 2029 — growth levels far beyond most current economic forecasts. Ross Hickey, an associate professor of economics and management at UBC Okanagan, says this type of growth is unlikely. He gave a “cautiously optimistic” forecast of one per cent GDP growth per year for the next three years. The Bank of Canada projects national GDP growth at 0.7 per cent this year, 1.8 per cent next year, and 1.8 per cent the year after that. The Royal Bank of Canada projects B.C.’s economy to grow 0.8 per cent this year and 1.5 per cent next year. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says his party will achieve these higher levels by “supercharging” the economy. “We are predicting roughly one per cent more optimism in this province than the NDP,” Doerkson said Monday. “And frankly, I think it’s completely achievable.” But Doerkson fails to explain how some of his promises, such as ending Clean BC or reducing permitting times, will create the growth surge he promises. items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alaska’s monster tsunami sent water 1,580 feet up a mountain
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. As glaciers retreat, similar disasters could become a growing danger in mountainous coastal regions.

items.title: [Nautilus] Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

With the advent of e-cigarettes, millions of smokers gained a way to get their nicotine fix without many of the negative health effects of lighting tobacco on fire. Of course, because the technology is relatively new, there’s plenty we don’t know about any other adverse long-term effects. That’s one reason it’s particularly troubling that young people have adopted vaping, too. Now the latest data on youth vaping trends is out, and it’s showing some interesting gender differences. 

In a letter published today in JAMA Pediatrics, a team of researchers from the Medical University of South Carolina reports that vaping is on the rise among girls. It’s a bit puzzling. For decades, the reverse was true—more men and boys indulged in nicotine products than women. But according to data from the youth cohort for the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) study, girls have been more likely to vape than boys since 2021, with a wider gap in older teens.

Read more: “How Nicotine Disrupts the “Lung-Brain Axis”—And Could Lead to Dementia”

The post Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys appeared first on Nautilus.
